posts.title: Gouged
posts.description: I heard about this book from Marketplace . I knew companies have been playing with prices online for ages, but now we're getting into the same games with in-person shopping in brick and mortar stores. We all want to feel that we're getting a fair price for whatever we're purchasing. When you feel like you're the subject of price manipulation that you as the consumer don't have any access to, and certainly can't predict with any measure of certainty, it just feels very unfair. Public trust collapses when prices become volatile, opaque, and constantly in flux. Participating in society, whether at work, in a neighborhood, or at a farmers market, depends on a shared set of rules. When those rules erode or norms shift, we're given the opportunity to re-evaluate what matters. In the face of the disappearing price tag and the rise of dynamic pricing, this is that moment. posts.title: Green & Deadly Things
posts.description: I got this book for my sci-fi/fantasy book club back in June, but due to my trip to New York I missed the book club and didn't end up reading the book until now. The book was a mostly enjoyable fantasy tale whose setup actually reminded me some of the Mistborn series by Brandon Sanderson, though without quite the depth that Sanderson adds to his books. But for this, the depth isn't needed and doesn't subtract from the story. The book had some good twists and turns with an ending that felt satisfying. I probably could've dealt without some the romance parts of the story, but still enjoyed the book overall. Thank you for reading this with RSS and keeping RSS alive! You're awesome! posts.title: The Wager
posts.description: I was recommended this book by Kai Ryssdal (the host of Marketplace) and I'm glad I borrowed this from the library. The story is of the HMS Wager , a British warship in the 1700s that was on a mission around Cape Horn on the southern tip of South America. The ship wrecked off the coast of Chile and the men were stranded on an island that became known as Wager Island. It involves a mutiny and two separate groups from the survivors surviving and eventually making their way back to Britain. David Grann does a great job of telling the story of the ship, and its survivors efforts to stay alive and survive with very few resources, and little knowledge on how to survive in what were horrific conditions. The book is based off the journals of John Bulkeley, John Byron, and others. It was a captivating story and one I hadn't heard of before. I really enjoyed the way Grann told it.
